A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OHIO research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison, including material reordered between appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on Reacher, robotic manipulation, vehicle routing, and supply-chain control, together with supplementary analyses in Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds Door Opening results comparing single-expert and combined-expert datasets in Appendix C.3 and Table 13.

M1.justification: The core OHIO pipeline and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. However, the stated supply-chain controller restricts its inventory-error sum to distribution nodes and replaces the warehouse bound c_i^t with C_p,i, defined as production capacity (v1 Equation 29; v2 Equation 33). These are local revisions to the written controller formulation; implementation changes are not established.

E1.justification: V2 Appendix C.3 adds expert-only Door Opening data and a combined dataset collected from three expert policies with different controller configurations. This extends training-data coverage to heterogeneous controller sources within an existing task. The robotics, urban-routing, and supply-chain domains are otherwise retained.

E2.justification: V2 Table 13 adds an evaluated hierarchical imitation-learning comparator, HIL, which learns both hierarchy levels through imitation. It compares HIL with OHIO-IL and, on combined data, HRL and OHIO-IQL. Comparator membership in the retained main experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new experiment uses 250 single-expert episodes and 600 combined episodes, comprising 200 from each of three controller configurations, with imitation and offline-RL comparisons. V2 also corrects the displayed supply-chain capacity-violation penalty from an effective addition to subtraction (v1 Equation 28; v2 Equation 32). The PDFs do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds an analysis of learning from limited expert demonstrations versus combined controller sources, including imitation-versus-RL comparisons. Existing inverse-solver, controller-robustness, reduced-data, capacity-transfer, runtime, and fine-tuning analyses remain present.

E5.justification: Both versions report scores with ± quantities and shaded learning curves. V2 extends the same reporting convention to Table 13 without adding run counts, seed information, uncertainty definitions, or statistical tests.

E6.justification: New Table 13 reports single-expert scores of 57.73±39.2 for HIL and 26.44±37.9 for OHIO-IL. Combined-expert scores are 29.89±34.8 for HIL, 64.75±37.7 for HRL, 81.85±33.1 for OHIO-IL, and 91.1±23.2 for OHIO-IQL. These are additional results under new settings. Tables 1–5, retained appendix results, and plotted data are unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix B.3.5 expands the routing inverse from a direct reconstruction formula into a primal formulation with slack variables and an inverse formulation minimizing the duality gap. It identifies bilinearity and states conditions under which the existing analytical solution applies. This adds mathematical reasoning without replacing the central inversion framework.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about offline hierarchical-policy reconstruction, improved performance and robustness, and safer deployment and fine-tuning. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.5 explicitly requires observed low-level actions when no approximate dynamics model is available. Appendix B.3.5 qualifies the simple routing inverse using feasibility and minimum-cost-flow conditions. Appendix C.3 adds an interpretation of limited expert-data coverage and the benefits of combining controller sources; the existing conclusion limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents finite-difference linearization and the LQR Riccati recursion in Appendix B.1, clarifies routing-baseline variables, and supplies the new expert-data collection recipe. Existing hardware and hyperparameter disclosures are retained. The code/data link moves from an experimental footnote to the abstract, without establishing a change in availability.

R1.justification: V2 adds Chan and Kaw (2020) to support inverse recovery of constraint parameters, removes Allgöwer and Zheng (2012), and explicitly attributes the network-control formulations to Gammelli et al. (2023). The broader related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized wording and terminology edits, adds explanatory comments to Algorithm 1, inserts Appendices A.5 and C.3, and swaps the vehicle-routing and supply-chain appendix sections. Publication and author-header text are updated, while the main narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 13 and redraws Figures 3–4 with changed node shading and arrow styling. Appendix displays are resized or relocated, including placing Figures 8–9 together, and the conference header changes page layout. The retained experimental plots use unchanged image content.

improvement.justification: V2 improves documentation of inversion requirements and mathematical reasoning, corrects the displayed reward-penalty sign, and adds useful evidence showing both weak single-expert performance and stronger combined-source results. These are limited gains: the principal evidence remains unchanged, the new dataset comparison changes sample size alongside source diversity, and the implementation implications of the revised supply-chain controller specification are not documented.
